e.correcta: Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that, in its yeast form at body temperature, appears as small (2-4 micrometer) oval yeasts that are classically found clustered within macrophages, exactly as depicted by the arrow in this image — this intracellular macrophage-parasitizing pattern is a key distinguishing feature. Histoplasmosis is endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys and is acquired by inhaling spores from soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings.

incorrectas.A: Blastomyces dermatitidis yeast forms are much larger (8-15 micrometers), thick-walled, and show broad-based budding, and they are typically extracellular rather than packed inside macrophages as shown here.
incorrectas.C: Cryptococcus neoformans yeasts have a thick polysaccharide capsule best visualized with India ink or mucicarmine stain, producing a halo around the yeast, and they are not classically found clustered within macrophages in this small uniform pattern.
incorrectas.D: Coccidioides immitis in tissue forms large spherules (30-60 micrometers) packed with endospores, a dramatically different and much larger morphology than the tiny yeast forms seen intracellularly here.

q: A KOH preparation of a skin scraping from a patient with hypopigmented, scaly patches on the trunk is shown, demonstrating short hyphae admixed with clusters of round yeast forms, described as a "spaghetti and meatballs" pattern. Which organism is responsible for this presentation?

e.correcta: Malassezia furfur (formerly Pityrosporum) is a dimorphic, lipophilic fungus that is part of normal skin flora but can cause tinea (pityriasis) versicolor, producing hypopigmented or hyperpigmented scaly patches, classically on the trunk. On KOH prep it shows the pathognomonic combination of short curved hyphae ("spaghetti") along with round yeast clusters ("meatballs"), exactly as depicted in this image.

incorrectas.A: Trichophyton rubrum is a dermatophyte causing tinea corporis, pedis, and onychomycosis; on KOH it shows septate hyphae without the yeast-cell clusters, lacking the "meatballs" component of the pattern shown.
incorrectas.B: Candida albicans forms pseudohyphae and budding yeast but does not produce the discrete short curved hyphae with round yeast clusters characteristic of the spaghetti-and-meatballs appearance, and it more classically causes mucocutaneous or vaginal infections rather than trunk hypopigmentation.
incorrectas.D: Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus causing sporotrichosis ("rose gardener's disease") with cigar-shaped yeast forms and nodular lymphocutaneous lesions following a traumatic inoculation, an entirely different clinical and morphologic picture.

q: On this ventral view of the brainstem, a dense fan of cranial nerve rootlets is shown emerging along the lateral medulla and pontomedullary junction. The boxed 'ID' label marks a rootlet exiting laterally right at the junction between the pons and the upper medulla, at the level where the diagram groups nerves V, VI, VII, and VIII. Which cranial nerve is this?

e.correcta: CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) emerges from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, at the cerebellopontine angle, immediately adjacent to CN VII. It carries special sensory fibers for hearing (cochlear division) and balance (vestibular division), and this exit point is clinically important because tumors here (vestibular schwannomas) classically compress both CN VII and CN VIII together, producing progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance.

incorrectas.A: CN VII (facial) exits right next to CN VIII at the same pontomedullary junction, but it runs slightly more medially/anteriorly toward the internal acoustic meatus and carries motor fibers to the muscles of facial expression rather than the special sensory fibers marked by the more posterolateral vestibulocochlear root shown here.
incorrectas.C: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) exits from the medulla more caudally, below the pontomedullary junction, as part of a series of rootlets alongside CN X and XI along the postolivary sulcus — its exit point is distinctly lower than the level marked in this image.
incorrectas.D: CN V (trigeminal) exits from the mid-pons as a large single root, well rostral to the pontomedullary junction — its position is clearly more superior than the rootlet marked here.

q: On this ventral view of the brainstem, the boxed 'ID' label sits over the smooth, oval surface bulge on the lateral medulla, just below the pontomedullary junction and lateral to the corticospinal tract (pyramid) that runs down the midline. Which structure produces this surface elevation?

e.correcta: The olive is the oval prominence on the ventrolateral medulla, produced by the underlying inferior olivary nucleus, which sits just lateral to the pyramid, posterior to the hypoglossal (CN XII) rootlets, and medial to the line of CN IX, X, and XI rootlets. The inferior olivary nucleus relays proprioceptive and motor-error signals to the contralateral cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle (climbing fibers), playing a key role in motor learning and coordination.

incorrectas.A: The cerebral peduncle is a midbrain structure carrying descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers on the ventral midbrain surface — it lies far rostral to the medulla, near the level labeled 'Midbrain III, IV' in this diagram, not at the medullary level marked here.
incorrectas.B: The facial colliculus is a small elevation on the dorsal (not ventral) surface of the pons, caused by the abducens nucleus and the looping facial nerve fibers around it — it is not visible on this ventral view and is unrelated to the lateral medullary bulge shown.
incorrectas.D: The gracile tubercle is a small dorsal medullary elevation overlying the nucleus gracilis, part of the dorsal column pathway — it belongs on the posterior surface of the brainstem, not the ventrolateral bulge highlighted here.

q: On this ventral view of the brainstem, the boxed 'ID' label marks a line of rootlets that arises along the lateral medulla and extends further caudally than the other rootlets shown, continuing down toward the upper cervical spinal cord near where the corticospinal tract (pyramid) descends. Which cranial nerve is this?

e.correcta: The accessory nerve (CN XI) has a unique dual origin: cranial rootlets from the caudal medulla and, more prominently, spinal rootlets that arise from the upper cervical spinal cord (roughly C1-C5) and ascend through the foramen magnum before joining the cranial root and exiting the skull via the jugular foramen. This is why its rootlets are seen extending down past the medulla into the cervical cord region, distinguishing it from the purely medullary cranial nerves positioned above it.

incorrectas.A: CN XII (hypoglossal) exits from the ventral medulla via the preolivary sulcus, medial to the olive and between the olive and the pyramid, not from the more lateral, caudally-extending line of rootlets marked here — its position is medial and its rootlets do not extend down into the spinal cord.
incorrectas.B: CN X (vagus) does exit from the lateral medulla along the postolivary sulcus, but its rootlets sit rostral to CN XI's, immediately below CN IX and confined to the medulla — the rootlets marked in this image extend caudal to that position, down toward the spinal cord, which is characteristic of CN XI rather than CN X.
incorrectas.C: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) is the most rostral of the postolivary sulcus rootlets, exiting just below the pontomedullary junction — it is positioned well above the rootlets marked here, which extend down into the upper cervical region.

q: On this rostral medulla cross-section, the labeled (ID) structure is the large oval region at the dorsal surface, medial to the inferior cerebellar peduncle and the entering CN VIII fibers, and just lateral/superior to the hypoglossal nucleus. Which structure is this?

e.correcta: The spinal trigeminal nucleus forms a long column running through the dorsolateral medulla, extending from the pons down to the upper cervical spinal cord, and at the rostral medulla it lies medial to the inferior cerebellar peduncle near the dorsal surface, adjacent to the hypoglossal nucleus. It receives pain and temperature fibers from the ipsilateral face via cranial nerves V, VII, IX, and X, mediating facial pain/temperature sensation analogous to the spinothalamic tract in the body; infarction here (e.g., lateral medullary/Wallenberg syndrome) causes loss of ipsilateral facial pain and temperature sensation.

incorrectas.A: The cochlear nucleus sits more laterally, right at the point where CN VIII fibers enter the brainstem alongside the inferior cerebellar peduncle, not medially near the hypoglossal nucleus as depicted here.
incorrectas.C: The nucleus ambiguus lies more ventrolaterally, near the origin of CN IX and X rootlets, and gives rise to motor fibers for the pharynx and larynx, not this dorsomedial position.
incorrectas.D: The inferior olivary nucleus is a large, ventrally located structure in the medulla (the prominent yellow oval in this diagram), quite distinct in both shape and position from the dorsally placed structure indicated here.

q: On this lateral diagram of the cerebral cortex, the 'ID' label marks a band in the frontal lobe that sits immediately anterior to the primary motor strip bordering the central sulcus (Rolando) — that is, caudal to the frontal eye field but rostral to the precentral gyrus. Damage to this band impairs the planning, sequencing, and coordination of complex, learned voluntary movements even though raw strength is preserved. Which cortical area is marked?

e.correcta: The premotor cortex (Brodmann area 6) forms a band on the lateral frontal lobe directly anterior to the primary motor cortex/central sulcus and caudal to the frontal eye field. It participates in planning and coordinating learned, sequential motor programs (often cued by external stimuli) before primary motor cortex executes them, and lesions here produce apraxia-like deficits in skilled movement despite intact strength.

incorrectas.A: The frontal eye field (area 8) lies rostral to the premotor band, closer to the middle frontal gyrus, and its main function is generating contralateral saccadic eye movements rather than coordinating limb motor programs.
incorrectas.B: Prefrontal association cortex occupies the anterior-most frontal lobe, well rostral to both the frontal eye field and the premotor band, and mediates executive function, judgment, and personality rather than movement planning.
incorrectas.D: Primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3, 1, 2) lies on the postcentral gyrus, posterior to the central sulcus in the parietal lobe, and processes touch, proprioception, and vibration rather than motor planning.

q: On this inferior view of the brain showing the circle of Willis and its branches, the labeled vessel ('ID') is seen arising laterally from the rostral basilar trunk, just below the internal carotid/posterior communicating artery junction, and coursing over the upper pons toward the cerebellar surface. Which artery is indicated?

e.correcta: The superior cerebellar artery (SCA) arises from the tip of the basilar artery just before it bifurcates into the two posterior cerebral arteries, making it sit immediately adjacent to the ICA/PCom/PCA junction seen in this figure — the exact reason its label is so easily mistaken for the PCA. From there it courses posterolaterally around the midbrain, just below the oculomotor nerve and above the trigeminal nerve root, to supply the superior surface of the cerebellum and part of the midbrain.

incorrectas.A: The posterior cerebral artery continues from the basilar bifurcation around the midbrain to supply the occipital and inferior temporal lobes; in this diagram it is the vessel that curves up and over into the temporal lobe from the ICA/PCom loop, one level above and separate from the vessel actually indicated here.
incorrectas.B: AICA arises from the proximal-to-mid basilar trunk, below the level of the SCA, and loops laterally near the cerebellopontine angle (near CN VII/VIII) — it sits lower on the trunk than the vessel labeled here, which branches right at the top of the basilar near the ICA/PCom junction.
incorrectas.D: PICA arises from the vertebral artery near the medulla, the most caudal of the three cerebellar arteries — on this figure it would be labeled much lower, near the medullary/vertebral segment, not at the upper pons-midbrain junction beside the internal carotid loop.

q: Which formula, shown in the image, is used to estimate the volume of distribution (Vd) of a drug?

o.B: Vd = (bioavailability x dose) / plasma concentration at time zero

e.correcta: The image depicts the standard equation Vd = amount of drug in the body / plasma drug concentration, which in practice is estimated as Vd = (F x dose) / Cp0, where F is bioavailability and Cp0 is the extrapolated plasma concentration at time zero. This formula conceptually asks how large a volume the drug would need to occupy, at the concentration measured in plasma, to account for the entire dose administered — a low Vd implies the drug stays mostly in the vasculature, while a high Vd implies extensive tissue distribution.

incorrectas.A: Clearance / elimination rate constant (CL/ke) is actually an alternative, mathematically equivalent way to calculate Vd, but it is not the formula shown in this image, which specifically depicts the dose-and-concentration-based definition.
incorrectas.C: Half-life is related to Vd and clearance by t1/2 = 0.693 x Vd / CL, but this expression calculates half-life, not volume of distribution itself, and does not match the equation pictured.
incorrectas.D: Maintenance dose / clearance describes how to calculate a steady-state plasma concentration or dosing rate, not the volume of distribution.

q: A patient returning from a trip to sub-Saharan Africa presents with cyclical fevers, chills, and malaise. A thin blood smear is obtained (image shown). The infected red blood cell is markedly enlarged and contains a dense, irregularly lobulated purple mass whose chromatin appears clumped into multiple segments, rather than a single delicate ring or one smooth ameboid form. Which Plasmodium life-cycle stage is shown?

e.correcta: This is a schizont: the infected RBC is enlarged and packed with a lobulated, segmented mass of dark purple chromatin representing multiple merozoite nuclei produced by asexual nuclear division of the parasite, rather than a single ring or solid ameboid blob. This stage is clinically important because the mature schizont ruptures the RBC, releasing merozoites that go on to invade new erythrocytes, driving the cyclical hemolysis and fever seen in malaria. Schizogony (this repeated cycle of merozoite release and reinvasion) underlies the periodic fever pattern used to help distinguish Plasmodium species.

incorrectas.A: A ring-form trophozoite appears as a thin, delicate loop of blue-purple cytoplasm with a single small chromatin dot, resembling a signet ring — it lacks the dense, multi-segmented chromatin mass seen here.
incorrectas.C: A gametocyte, especially in P. falciparum, has a distinctive elongated, crescent (banana) shape; the parasite in this image instead nearly fills a rounded, unruptured RBC with clumped internal segments, which does not fit a gametocyte's morphology.
incorrectas.D: An early (ameboid) trophozoite shows irregular, amoeba-like cytoplasmic extensions with a single nucleus and no division into discrete chromatin clumps, whereas this parasite already shows evidence of nuclear segmentation into multiple merozoite-forming units.

review_note: The merozoites appear as a clumped, lobulated mass rather than cleanly separated individual dots, so an exact merozoite count cannot be confidently read off this image; the description above reflects the overall segmented, multi-nucleated appearance actually observed rather than a precise count.

q: The image lists a group of anti-HIV drugs (abacavir, didanosine, emtricitabine, lamivudine, stavudine, tenofovir, zidovudine). Most of these agents do not share a single common name suffix (only lamivudine, stavudine, and zidovudine end in "-vudine"), but all of them require intracellular phosphorylation before competing with natural nucleotides for incorporation into viral DNA. Which drug class do they belong to?

e.correcta: All seven drugs (abacavir, didanosine, emtricitabine, lamivudine, stavudine, tenofovir, zidovudine) are nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs). They are synthetic nucleoside (or nucleotide) analogs that must be phosphorylated intracellularly to their active triphosphate forms before competing with endogenous nucleotides for incorporation by HIV reverse transcriptase, acting as chain terminators because they lack the 3'-OH group needed to form the next phosphodiester bond. Unlike most drug classes, NRTIs do not have one universal naming suffix: "-vudine" identifies only lamivudine, stavudine, and zidovudine, while abacavir, didanosine, emtricitabine, and tenofovir are naming outliers that must simply be memorized as belonging to this class.

incorrectas.A: NNRTIs (e.g., efavirenz, nevirapine) also inhibit reverse transcriptase, but they bind an allosteric site on the enzyme directly rather than acting as nucleoside/nucleotide analogs, so they do not require intracellular phosphorylation and are structurally unrelated to the drugs listed here.
incorrectas.B: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (e.g., raltegravir, dolutegravir, bictegravir) block the integrase enzyme from inserting proviral DNA into the host genome, a later step in the HIV life cycle that has nothing to do with reverse transcriptase or nucleotide competition.
incorrectas.C: Protease inhibitors (e.g., ritonavir, indinavir, saquinavir, atazanavir) inhibit the HIV protease enzyme responsible for cleaving polyprotein precursors into mature structural and enzymatic proteins, acting at a much later stage of viral maturation than reverse transcription.
